newsitem.title: USA: Motorola launches policy against land mines.
newsitem.headline: Motorola launches policy against land mines.

text.p: Technology giant Motorola Inc. Monday banned sales of one of its switches for use in making land mines, joining a U.S.-led international crusade against the concealed killers of tens of thousands of people every year.

"When we found out this product was being used for that purpose, we began an internal review to determine how it happened and what we could do to be sure our product would not be used in that fashion in the future," Larry Barton, Motorola's vice president of issues management, said in a telephone interview.
Under the policy, the Schaumburg, Ill.-based company will not knowingly sell switches known as common logic devices to land mine manufacturers or to companies that supply them.
The switch is used in tens of thousands of household products ranging from washing machines to hair dryers -- but is also an integral part of anti-personnel mines.
The use of the Motorola switches in mines came to light in a summer edition of the Public Broadcasting Services science programme "Nova."
"In that programme, they showed an individual opening a land mine that was found, and in there was one of these devices," Barton said, adding that Motorola was named. "That was a real eye-opener."

Motorola insisted that it was never in the land mine business. Barton said the devices were largely sold to land mine manufacturers by resellers such as overstocked computer producers. However, an internal investigation discovered Motorola had sold to one land-mine manufacturer which corporate headquarters had been previously unaware of.
"Some companies who manufacture land mines and some countries clearly were able to access our product," Barton said, declining to give names.

International pressure to ban land mines has been growing. At the United Nations General Assembly, speakers have lined up to denounce the mines and to appeal for fresh efforts to ban their manufacture, stockpiling and use.

"We must end the carnage caused by anti-personnel landmines -- the hidden killers that murder and maim more than 25,000 people every year," President Clinton said in a speech to the assembly last Tuesday. "... Our children deserve to walk this Earth in safety."

CARE relief agency spokeswoman Wendy Driscoll, citing U.N. figures, said Monday some 110 million land mines are scattered in 64 countries and about 2 million more are planted every year. The mines cost about $3 each to make and $1,200 each to clear.

"Until recently, land mine production has been tolerated in most countries," Driscoll said. "Motorola's decision ... really sends a message. I think a lot of (companies) are unaware and what Motorola has done is open the door to question how and where their products are used."
Motorola said it did not expect its policy, which has been in development since June, to affect its bottom line.
The policy includes education of its sales force and simply not selling the switches when there is any question as to how they will be used.

"Obviously it was not a huge issue for us from a financial perspective," said Barton, who called the price of the switches "minuscule." Motorola, with revenues of $27 billion last year, is a leader in the semiconductor and cellular phone markets.
"It was very much a question of our senior management and employees and even their families being very disturbed by a use of our product we found abhorrent," Barton said.
